Otter documents its Public API in a single help-center article ("Otter.ai Public API"): "Otter's Public API provides programmatic access to retrieve channels, conversations, transcripts, audio, action items, insights, outlines, and workspace details", "available for all Enterprise workspaces", base URL https://api.otter.ai/v1 with API-key auth. The article is prose with static examples: no machine-readable spec is published (api.otter.ai/openapi.json 404), no interactive reference, no sandbox, and no version lifecycle beyond the /v1 path. (The article HTML sits behind a Cloudflare challenge; this is the same host's public help-center JSON endpoint.)

Original poster: the Otter bot joined two confidential meetings on their behalf, recorded them, and emailed every member an "absurd, inaccurate 'outline'" afterward. They opened a support ticket with screenshots but got no response. According to Twitter, Otter was not reviewing tickets from free users at the time.

"I just deleted my account because of that, also they share conversations with everyone in the meeting by DEFAULT, it wasn't nice receiving a message from a co-worker telling me that he received an email with the transcription it generated."

One user stopped using Otter after seeing it shares notes with everyone by default. They wanted notes only for themselves so they could be more present in meetings, not to make everyone feel they had to watch what they said because it was being transcribed.

One user relies on Otter exclusively for voice journaling. Between the consent news and recent UI changes that made the record/stop button tiny in the iOS app, they are looking for an alternative. DayOne's voice limits are too short for them.
Reacting to the Otter bot recording meetings without consent, one commenter said: "This is why I use Clari Wingman instead."

A commenter was in a confidential meeting where a lawyer had invited OtterAI. After reading Otter's privacy statement, they understood that recordings are retained in the cloud and used, "anonymized," as training data. They doubted Otter's ability to secure and truly anonymize the data and refused to continue with the bot present.

Someone in a child-related lawsuit had a lawyer use Otter to record a very confidential meeting. Their first awareness of the recording was a summary email at the end of the meeting. When asked, the company dismissed responsibility and said it was up to subscribers to use the product appropriately.

"I remember being on sensitive zoom calls and seeing Otter.ai join. Had to track down which person was using it, and even they were clueless as to how it got there, and the client kept rejoining despite the user trying to stop it."
Asked why Otter exists when videoconferencing apps have built-in transcription, a commenter replied: "Most of the ones built into the video conferencing solutions aren't as good."

A self-described cloud hater admits "Otter is very good." They used it with someone on AirPods over a poor internet connection with no noticeable drop in accuracy, and it even spelled uncommon last names correctly.
One user checked NetGuard and found the Otter Android app had connected to the internet 6 times since they last opened it.
"Otter is the only thing approaching affordable for individuals, but I don't really trust it given they're playing fast and loose with user data." The commenter is looking for an offline alternative.

One user records all their work meetings with Otter and finds it great for going back to details they didn't take notes on. It doesn't do an amazing job with varied English accents on their distributed team; they find Google Recorder on Android better there. Still: "good enough. Nice product."

"Disclosure: have used Otter, like it, but wary of security issues. Self hosted option sounds good." The commenter notes that automated recording means sending recordings to a cloud you don't control, which is a bad idea for sensitive content.

Original poster says the Otter.ai bot joined two confidential meetings on their behalf, recorded them, then emailed every member an "absurd, inaccurate 'outline'" afterward. A support ticket with screenshots got no response, reportedly because tickets from free users weren't being reviewed.
Deleted account because Otter shares conversations with everyone in the meeting by default; a co-worker messaged them after receiving an email with the transcription Otter generated.

Stopped using Otter after learning it shares with everyone by default. Wanted the notes only for themselves so they could be more present in meetings, not at the expense of making everyone feel they had to watch what they said.
User who relies on Otter exclusively for voice journaling is seeking an alternative, citing the bot news and recent iOS UI changes that made the record/stop button tiny.
Commenters recommend alternatives: one uses Clari Wingman instead of Otter, another uses Avoma for sales because of its "very tight controls."
A potential customer's Otter.ai agent auto-joined a Teams call. The customer never showed, but two others chatted, and Otter posted a link to a full recording, including video of their faces.

Same EU user filed a GDPR deletion request. The listed privacy email bounced unless sent from an Otter account. Support cited the CCPA, said to contact the conversation owner, and then stopped replying after escalation. The user is now filing a lawsuit.

Non-user says Otter sent meeting notes to all attendees appearing to come "from me" and showed them inviting Otter to private work meetings, despite having no account. They describe it as "like a virus" and are trying to figure out how to stop it.
Contrarian view: commenter sides with Otter, arguing it recorded the call and sent the recording to all participants, and "it's not their fault the users are idiots."

Long-time user records all work meetings with Otter and finds it great for going back to details they didn't note. It doesn't handle varied English accents amazingly well (Google Recorder on Android is better there) but is "good enough"; calls it a nice product.
At an education company, Otter in Zoom transcribed an instructor's slightly garbled "I think that" as "I Fuck That" in front of middle schoolers.

Commenter says Otter is the only option approaching affordable for individuals, but they don't trust it because it's "playing fast and loose with user data." They are looking for an offline alternative.
Commenter argues the article about Otter's survey was sensationalist. The survey only referenced a recording title the reporter typed himself, and they see "no appearance of foul play" by Otter.

Commenter flags inconsistent answers from Otter staff on whether it shares user data with non-US governments or law enforcement. One rep cited legal disclosure obligations while another said the opposite, suggesting no consistent internal policy.

Commenter recommends Microsoft Word online's Transcription feature as an alternative for transcribing recorded work calls (300 min/month with Microsoft 365), though it struggles with transcripts longer than 50 pages.

Team switched to Bluedot, a bot-free Otter alternative, a couple of months ago. They report a productivity boost from reviewing client meetings and are starting to use it as a knowledge base for their dev team.
